sentences.text: Tenzin lived in a small village in the Bumthang valley, in central Bhutan.

It was a quiet place — maybe two hundred people, a handful of farms, a small school, one bakery, one general store, and, on the highest ridge behind the village, a small monastery where seventeen monks lived.
Tenzin's grandfather was one of those monks, though he did not live in the monastery in the village — he lived in a much smaller monastery, much higher up, two days' walk into the mountains.

His grandfather was Grandfather Rinpoche, but everyone in Tenzin's family called him Grandfather Rinpoche because he was both — he was a grandfather, and he was a rinpoche, which was an old title of respect for a Buddhist monk who had studied for many years.
He was seventy-six years old.
He had lived at the high monastery for forty-one years.
Before that he had been married, briefly, and had had Tenzin's mother.
Tenzin's grandmother had died young, and after her death Grandfather Rinpoche had gone into the monastery.
That was the whole story, more or less.
Tenzin's mother had grown up mostly with her aunt in the village.
She had always loved her father and had never resented his choice.
Tenzin was eleven, and this was the third summer he had walked to the high monastery alone.
His mother had said, when he was nine, that he could go alone starting when he was ten.
The path was not dangerous — it was well-marked and well-used, and there were two small villages along the way where he stopped to eat and to sleep.
But it was two days' walk, and it climbed steeply from 2,700 meters at the village to 3,400 meters at the monastery.
Tenzin was strong for his age.
He liked the walk.
He looked forward to it all year.
This July he had left the village at first light on a Monday morning.
He carried a small canvas pack with a change of clothes, some dried food, a water bottle, and a small paper-wrapped gift for his grandfather — his mother had made a small woolen scarf.
It was still cool.
Bhutan in July was the beginning of the monsoon, which meant it rained heavily most afternoons and was misty most mornings.
Tenzin walked.
He knew the path.
He passed the first small village at midmorning.
He passed the second one at noon and stopped there for a hot meal.
In the afternoon he continued upward, into the pine forest, into the mist.
He slept that first night at a small pilgrim's hut halfway up.
There were two other travelers there — an older monk on his way down to the village, and a woman making a pilgrimage to a specific shrine.
They shared a small fire and simple food.
Tenzin was very tired.
He slept without dreams.
In the morning he continued up.
The path got steeper.
The trees got smaller.
The air got thinner.
In the afternoon of the second day he came up over a ridge and there — across a deep valley — was the monastery.
It was very small.
Whitewashed walls, red and gold trim, prayer flags on the roof.
It clung to the side of a rocky outcrop as if it had grown there.
Beyond it, the great snow peaks of the Himalayas rose into the deep blue sky.
Tenzin stopped for a moment.
He had seen the monastery every summer for three years but every time he stopped at this same spot.
It was one of the most beautiful views in the world.
He arrived at the monastery gate at four in the afternoon.
Grandfather Rinpoche was waiting at the gate.
He had known Tenzin was coming.
Tenzin's mother had sent a message through a monk going up the previous week.
Grandfather Rinpoche was small and thin and had a shaved head.
He wore the maroon and saffron robes of a Bhutanese monk.
He looked much like the other monks in the monastery.
But his eyes were Tenzin's grandfather's eyes.
He put his hand on Tenzin's shoulder.
He said, in his soft voice, "You made it, boy.
Come.
You need tea.
You need food.
You need rest.
In that order.
Everything else can wait." Tenzin gave him the small wrapped scarf.
Grandfather Rinpoche opened it.
He put it around his neck immediately.
He said, "Beautiful.
Your mother's hands.
Tell her when you see her that I wore it the first day.
Come."
The monastery was small — one main building, one prayer hall, one kitchen, and a row of small cells for the monks to sleep in.
There were seven monks living there full-time, and usually a few visiting monks or pilgrims.
Tenzin would sleep in a small guest cell near his grandfather's.
He had done this three summers now.
He knew the routine.
Meals at fixed times.
Chanting in the early morning and at dusk.
Small work in the middle of the day — gardening, sweeping, tending the small chapel.
Long periods of silence.
Tenzin liked the routine.
He liked the silence best.
That evening after supper, Grandfather Rinpoche took Tenzin outside onto the stone terrace at the front of the monastery.
The sun was setting behind the great peaks.
The whole world was pink and gold.
Grandfather Rinpoche said, "This summer, Tenzin.
I want to give you something.
Not tonight.
In a few days.
But I want you to know I have something for you.
I have been waiting for the right summer.
This is it.
You will be twelve in the winter, correct?" Tenzin said, "Yes.
In December." Grandfather Rinpoche nodded.
He said, "Then this is the right summer.
Rest tonight.
Tomorrow we talk."
